content:
Hundreds of flights across the northeastern United States were cancelled due to a technical issue at a major regional air traffic control centre, as all major airports in New York City came to a standstill for several hours on Monday while world leaders flew in for the United Nations General Assembly.

However, President Trump's flight from Washington to New York departed on schedule.

The technical problem occurred at the same Federal Aviation Administration facility in Philadelphia that had caused repeated disruptions at Newark Liberty International Airport earlier in spring 2025.

These kinds of regional control centres have two lines responsible for transmitting data: a primary line and a backup line. The Federal Aviation Administration said a circuit on the primary line failed early Monday morning, and when the system attempted to switch to the backup, workers discovered the fibre-optic line had been cut. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed a crew of Amtrak engineers for the incident.

The outage affected flights at Philadelphia as well as Kennedy, LaGuardia and Newark airports.

By early afternoon, some flights at LaGuardia, Kennedy and Philadelphia began resuming, but significant delays were still expected throughout the day.

Some airlines allowed passengers to rebook their flights free of charge. The Federal Aviation Administration advised travellers to check flight status with their airlines before heading to the airport.

Federal Aviation Administration administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters the agency was working to install a new circuit on the primary line as soon as possible to restore primary line connectivity, while also rushing to repair the backup fibre-optic line, but was unable to determine how long it would take. Verizon said its technicians were working to restore service as quickly as possible.

"It could take 13 hours to fix the fibre break, it's a massive undertaking," Bedford said, according to a video posted online by a CBS News transportation reporter. He said the Federal Aviation Administration might be able to install a new circuit to restore primary line operations before the fibre-optic line was repaired.

The failed primary circuit will be replaced as part of a nationwide overhaul of the air traffic control system.

Also on Monday, the Federal Aviation Administration began testing a new computer system using artificial intelligence to help predict flight scheduling conflicts and weather issues so air traffic controllers can reroute planes. But that system is only in initial testing in Washington, D.C., so it does not appear to be related to the shutdown.
